paper_title: Fast Thermal Goodness Evaluation of a 3D-IC Floorplan

extraction.paper_title: Fast Thermal Goodness Evaluation of a 3D-IC Floorplan

scenario.figure_or_table: Figure 9 (thermal map of two 4-layer n100 3D floorplans, FP1 and FP2), with Figure 6 (TGV vs HotSpot peak temperature correlation for n100)
scenario.description: Comparison of two sample 4-layer 3D floorplans (FP1 and FP2) of the GSRC n100 benchmark, evaluating the power-based thermal goodness value (TGV) against HotSpot steady-state peak temperature. Module power densities were randomly assigned in the 1e5-1e7 W/m2 range and are not published per module; no block coordinates or per-block powers are given in the text. The heat sink is on top of the 4-layer stack, and layer 0 is farthest from the sink and hottest.
scenario.architecture: 4-layer TSV-based 3D IC, GSRC n100 benchmark floorplans generated by an evolutionary non-deterministic 3D floorplanner co-placing TSV islands and modules; 45 nm technology assumed; heat sink on top of stack
scenario.workload: No real workload; random per-module power densities (1e5-1e7 W/m2) held fixed across experiments; TSV islands treated as zero-power modules
scenario.operating_point: Steady-state HotSpot evaluation with default parameters on 64x64x4 grid (also 128 and 256 grids); example peak temperatures of 564 K (FP1) and 567 K (FP2) in Figure 10 for floorplans of 0.319 and 0.326 mm2

original_setup.solver: HotSpot (steady-state, default parameters) on a 64x64x4 grid, also run at 128 and 256 grids. It is compared against the proposed power-based thermal goodness value (TGV) evaluator. Heat sink is on top of the 4-layer stack.
original_setup.optimizer: Non-deterministic evolutionary 3D floorplanner that co-places TSV islands and modules. It builds on a sequence-pair 3D floorplanner and ELF-SP (refs 13-15). It only generated the floorplans; the paper's contribution is the TGV evaluator, not an optimizer run.
original_setup.controller: None. The paper uses no dynamic thermal controller or runtime thermal management.
original_setup.benchmark: GSRC n100, with FP1 and FP2 as the two 4-layer sample floorplans in Figure 9 (PDF page 5). 45 nm assumed, random module power densities of 1e5-1e7 W/m2 that are not published per module.

thermal_observable.location: Peak temperature of the 4-layer stack in HotSpot. Layer 0, farthest from the top heat sink, is the hottest layer in both FP1 and FP2.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Maximum steady-state temperature over the whole 3D floorplan, one value per floorplan. FP1 and FP2 values are shown only graphically in Figure 9, with no numeric text. Figure 10 on PDF page 6 gives 564 K and 567 K for two highlighted floorplans, but the packet does not confirm they are the Figure 9 FP1 and FP2.

physical_mismatches.reason: The scenario is a 4-layer TSV-based 3D stack with inter-layer heat flow and TSV islands. A planar or 2D steady-state Studio model cannot represent the vertical layer coupling that decides which layer is hottest.

The paper's primary metric is a non-physical power-based TGV (W/m2) that is not a temperature. It is validated only by correlation with HotSpot peak temperature, so there is no published absolute temperature field to replicate.
Module power densities were randomly assigned from 1e5-1e7 W/m2 and are not published. Block geometry and per-block powers for FP1 and FP2 are not given, so a faithful thermal setup cannot be built.

Layer thicknesses (Si, BEOL SiO2, TIM), heat-sink configuration, and the TSV island thermal treatment are only described qualitatively. HotSpot 'default parameters' are not specified in the paper. TSV islands are treated as zero-power modules in TGV.

The paper has no transient analysis, no controller, and no reliability analysis, so those aspects have nothing to compare against. The optimizer is a floorplanner, not a thermal controller, and does not map to a steady-state solve.

methods.note: The paper describes a power-based TGV compared against HotSpot on 4-layer 3D floorplans (pp.2-5). The extraction sets experiment.kind to custom_2d_steady while also marking steady_2d_relevant false and listing 3D vertical coupling as essential. That is a 2D label on a 3D problem. The scenario also merges Figure 9 (p.5) with Figure 10 (p.6) peak temperatures, and the paper does not say these are the same FP1/FP2.

code.note: The paper says the tools were written in C++ (p.4), but no code, repository or supplement is linked. artifact_search_status is checked_no_links and the assets list is empty. Nothing can be run or checked.

parameters.note: Several values are text-verified: 45 nm and 1e5-1e7 W/m2 (p.2), Table 1 runtimes and 22.2X (p.4), r=0.89 (p.4), r=0.96 (p.5), success rates 97%/87% (p.6), and 564/567 K with 0.319/0.326 mm2 (p.6). The exponents in the power range come from a garbled 'pdftotext' line ('105 -107') and are inferred as 10^5 to 10^7. No per-module power densities, layer thicknesses (Si, SiO2, TIM), TSV island sizes or HotSpot 'default parameters' are given, so the decisive simulation inputs are unavailable.

config.note: The heat sink is on top and layer 0 is the hottest (pp.2, 5). Beyond that, the die dimensions, stacking order, HotSpot material, convection and ambient settings, and random seed are not published. Studio package and material assumptions are empty. A 2D steady Studio configuration cannot represent the 4-layer stack with TSV islands.

assessment.summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable (simulation_allowed=false, comparison_valid=false). Studio did not run; the simulation status is skipped because the custom experiment has no blocks and no power_w object. The scenario is a 4-layer TSV-based 3D stack (GSRC n100, FP1/FP2, Figure 9 with Figure 6 correlation context), evaluated with HotSpot steady-state peak temperature against a power-based thermal goodness value (TGV). The proposed experiment kind was custom_2d_steady, which has no transient trace and would not represent vertical inter-layer coupling or TSV islands. Block geometry, per-block powers, and HotSpot configuration are unpublished. No Studio output exists, so no numerical comparison with the paper is possible or valid. The only paper temperatures are 564 K and 567 K from Figure 10. They are whole-stack HotSpot peaks, and their identity with the Figure 9 FP1/FP2 is unconfirmed. Qualitatively, the paper reports layer 0, farthest from the top heat sink, as the hottest layer. It also reports that TGV correlates with HotSpot peak temperature (r=0.89 for n100, 0.96 across all GSRC benchmarks). These are paper-reported findings, not results reproduced here. The gate also records unresolved adversarial and independent-review checks and evidence entries lacking valid page or asset locators. No claim of replication or agreement can be made.
limitations: Gate verdict not_2d_applicable: Studio was not run (status skipped), so there is no simulated result to compare.
Custom 2D steady setup would have no transient trace and cannot capture vertical layer coupling or TSV islands in a 4-layer stack.

Mismatches in location, aggregation, regime and boundary assumptions prevent any numeric comparison: the paper's peak is a 3D whole-stack maximum, with an unspecified HotSpot default package, heat sink, ambient and TSV treatment.
The paper's 564 K and 567 K Figure 10 peaks are not confirmed to correspond to Figure 9 FP1 and FP2; Figure 9 gives only a graphical thermal map with no numeric values.
The primary paper metric (TGV in W/m2) is not a temperature, so it cannot be validated by a Studio temperature output.
